paragraphs: An agent learning through reinforcement needs both a useful representation of its surroundings and useful behaviors that extend across multiple steps. This paper connects those challenges through proto-value functions, an existing representation-learning approach. It shows how these representations implicitly define options: extended behaviors that the agent can use while interacting with an environment.

The connection comes from eigenpurposes, intrinsic reward functions derived from the learned representation. These rewards encourage options that traverse principal directions of the state space. Instead of building each behavior around the environment’s task reward, the method extracts behaviors from the structure represented by the proto-value functions.

That separation from task rewards makes the discovered options useful across multiple tasks. The options also operate over different durations, giving exploration behaviors at different time scales. The paper demonstrates features of eigenpurposes in tabular environments and Atari 2600 games. Its contribution is a framework linking representation learning to reusable behavior discovery, with demonstrations across these two settings.
icml-2017-a-laplacian-framework-for-opti.tldr: Eigenpurposes turn learned state representations into task-independent, multistep behaviors useful for exploration.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder learns a probability model of observations using underlying latent variables. Its quality depends strongly on the inference model, which estimates those variables from an observation. This paper introduces Adversarial Variational Bayes to allow arbitrarily expressive inference models, addressing a restriction that can affect the resulting generative model.

The method adds an auxiliary discriminative network and uses it to express maximum-likelihood training as a game between two players. This provides a principled connection between variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks. The discriminator therefore plays a role in the inference and training formulation, rather than being an unrelated addition to the model.

The strongest result applies in the nonparametric limit: the method yields both exact maximum-likelihood generative parameters and the exact posterior over latent variables for an observation. That qualification matters when interpreting the exactness claim. The authors also describe the approach as easy to implement and retaining most standard VAE advantages, combining greater inference flexibility with a theoretical justification.
icml-2017-adversarial-variational-bayes-.tldr: Adversarial Variational Bayes uses a discriminative network to train VAEs with arbitrarily expressive inference models.

paragraphs: Learning from a data stream involves more than repeatedly adding observations to a fixed dataset. The model must keep updating while the process producing the data may itself change. This paper develops a Bayesian approach to those linked problems, covering a general class of conjugate exponential models.

The approach explicitly represents changes in model parameters over time through hierarchical priors. Those priors are non-conjugate, meaning they do not preserve the convenient mathematical relationships that make inference straightforward in the underlying conjugate models. This introduces a computational challenge alongside the benefit of directly modeling temporal change.

The authors derive a variational inference scheme that handles these priors while maintaining the computational efficiency associated with variational methods for conjugate models. They validate the approach on three real datasets using three latent-variable models. The contribution is therefore both a way to express changing stream behavior and an inference procedure intended to make that flexibility practical for continuous model updating.
icml-2017-bayesian-models-of-data-stream.tldr: Hierarchical priors model temporal changes in streaming data while a new variational scheme keeps inference computationally efficient.

paragraphs: Network traffic summaries may reveal how often each location is visited without revealing which connections people traverse. ChoiceRank addresses the problem of estimating transition probabilities along edges from these aggregate node counts. It formulates navigation as preference learning, using a model in which choices obey Luce’s axiom.

Under that model, the node-level visit counts are sufficient statistics for the transition probabilities. This is a substantial compression: the abstract describes O(n) counts supporting inference about O(n²) probabilities. The claim depends on the choice model; it does not mean that arbitrary patterns of network movement can be recovered from node totals alone.

The paper shows how to make inference well-posed regardless of network structure and introduces an iterative algorithm that scales to billions of nodes and edges. Two clickstream applications demonstrate successful recovery using network structure and node-level traffic. An additional application uses one year of New York City bicycle-sharing rides, extending the investigation from web navigation to mobility.
icml-2017-choicerank-identifying-prefere.tldr: ChoiceRank estimates network transition probabilities from aggregate node traffic under a Luce choice model.

paragraphs: A dynamically routed neural network can send different inputs through different sequences of learned transformations. The network is a graph with multiple possible paths, so its computation depends on the signal being processed. This paper proposes and systematically evaluates three strategies for training networks with that kind of input-dependent routing.

The comparison finds that some training approaches have advantages over others, but their resulting networks are often qualitatively similar. In image classification, layers and branches specialize in different image categories. This finding gives a concrete interpretation of the learned paths: different parts of the network develop distinct processing roles associated with the inputs they receive.

The authors also compare performance under a fixed computational budget. Dynamically routed networks tend to outperform comparable networks with static routing in that setting. The stated finding is a tendency, rather than a universal guarantee. Together, the results connect input-dependent computation with observed specialization and suggest that routing can improve how a network uses limited computation.
icml-2017-deciding-how-to-decide-dynamic.tldr: Dynamically routed networks develop specialized branches and tend to improve image classification under a fixed computational budget.

paragraphs: A summary of a data stream can lose useful elements when the people who supplied them withdraw permission to use their data. This paper studies how to maintain useful summaries when selected elements can be deleted. It formalizes that challenge as dynamic deletion-robust submodular maximization, making deletions part of the summarization problem itself.

The authors introduce ROBUST-STREAMING, described as the first resilient streaming algorithm for this problem. It provides a constant-factor approximation guarantee relative to the optimal solution. The guarantee establishes a bounded relationship to the best achievable objective value, rather than promising that the algorithm always constructs an optimal summary.

The evaluation covers streams of geographic coordinates, images, and clickstream logs. The clickstream application contains 45 million feature vectors from a news recommendation task. These applications examine the method across different forms of streaming data. The central contribution is a streaming summarization approach with a formal quality guarantee designed to accommodate the removal of data used in a summary.
icml-2017-deletion-robust-submodular-max.tldr: ROBUST-STREAMING builds deletion-resilient data summaries with a constant-factor approximation guarantee.

paragraphs: Running a neural network across different hardware devices requires deciding where its computations should execute. Those choices are often made by experts using heuristics and intuition. This paper treats placement as a learning problem for TensorFlow computational graphs, aiming to automate decisions about distributing operations across available devices.

A sequence-to-sequence model predicts placements for subsets of graph operations. The proposed placement is executed, and its execution time supplies the reward signal used to optimize the placement model. This connects the learning objective directly to runtime: the model receives feedback from how its proposed allocation actually performs.

The reported results cover Inception-V3 for ImageNet classification and LSTM recurrent networks for language modeling and neural machine translation. On those workloads, the method discovers nontrivial placements that outperform handcrafted heuristics and traditional algorithmic approaches. These findings show that learned placement can improve execution decisions in the evaluated settings, making hardware allocation another part of the neural-network workflow that can be optimized from experience.
icml-2017-device-placement-optimization-.tldr: A reinforcement-trained sequence model learns device placements that improve runtime over manual and algorithmic alternatives on the evaluated networks.

paragraphs: Topic models explain documents through underlying topics, but inference becomes harder as the models become more expressive. Traditional approaches seek closed-form update rules, which can make that growing complexity difficult to manage. This paper develops neural approaches that make topic-model training compatible with backpropagation through neural variational inference.

The method supplies parameterizable distributions over topics, allowing neural training machinery to carry out the inference process. It also introduces a recurrent network using a stick-breaking construction. That construction lets the model discover a notionally unbounded number of topics, giving it an analogy to Bayesian nonparametric topic models rather than requiring its conceptual topic capacity to stop at a fixed count.

Experiments on MXM Song Lyrics, 20NewsGroups, and Reuters News demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed neural topic models. The results support the combination of flexible topic representations and trainable inference on these document collections. The contribution brings both backpropagation-based training and an expandable topic construction into the same modeling direction.
icml-2017-discovering-discrete-latent-to.tldr: Neural variational inference trains topic models by backpropagation, including a recurrent model with notionally unbounded topic capacity.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks face difficulty learning relationships across long sequences. One proposed remedy constrains the transition matrix to be unitary, keeping its norm at one to prevent exploding gradients. The paper identifies a computational problem with existing approaches: they can restrict expressiveness or scale poorly, particularly when training uses small minibatches.

The authors first show how a unitary transition constraint can be viewed as a special case of an orthogonal constraint. They then introduce a parameterization based on Householder reflections that keeps the transition matrix orthogonal throughout training. The key design goal is to maintain the constraint while allowing efficient training of the recurrent network.

Their results show benefits similar to those of the unitary constraint without the associated time-complexity limitations. This makes the parameterization itself an important part of the contribution: a useful matrix constraint must also be affordable to maintain during optimization. The findings support an efficient route to the reported benefits of constrained recurrent transitions.
icml-2017-efficient-orthogonal-parametri.tldr: A Householder-based parameterization keeps recurrent transition matrices orthogonal while avoiding the time-complexity limitations of existing unitary approaches.

paragraphs: Archetypal Analysis seeks interpretable matrix factorizations by representing each data point as a convex combination of factors. Such combinations use nonnegative weights that sum to one. The factors lie on the boundary of the data’s convex hull, tying the representation to the outer geometry of the observed data while making computation expensive.

This paper focuses on the frame, the set of vertices defining that convex hull. The authors show that it can be computed efficiently using a quadratic program and provide both theoretical and empirical results for their approach. They then use the computed frame to accelerate Archetypal Analysis.

The resulting method achieves reconstruction errors similar to those of the baseline competitors while taking much less time to compute. That comparison matters because speed alone would be less useful if the factorization stopped representing the data well. The stated results indicate that exploiting the frame can preserve comparable reconstruction quality while reducing the computational burden of this interpretable factorization approach.
icml-2017-frame-based-data-factorization.tldr: Computing convex-hull vertices with a quadratic program accelerates Archetypal Analysis while retaining comparable reconstruction error.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential optimization of an unknown function under the assumption that it has a finite Lipschitz constant. That constant bounds how quickly function values can change with distance. The goal is to choose successive evaluations efficiently while requiring only this regularity assumption for the basic problem.

The authors identify sufficient conditions for consistency of generic sequential methods and formulate an expected minimax performance rate. They introduce LIPO for the case where the Lipschitz constant is known, proving consistency and minimax rates. Faster rates require an additional Hölder-like condition, so those stronger results rely on more structure than the basic Lipschitz assumption.

An adaptive version estimates the Lipschitz constant while optimizing, addressing the setting where the bound is initially unknown. Similar theoretical guarantees are established for this version. Numerical comparisons on standard global-optimization benchmarks illustrate the strategy’s potential relative to existing methods. The contribution combines formal performance analysis with an adaptive procedure that removes the need to supply the constant in advance.
icml-2017-global-optimization-of-lipschi.tldr: LIPO and its adaptive variant provide theoretically analyzed strategies for optimizing unknown Lipschitz functions through sequential evaluations.

paragraphs: Gibbs sampling repeatedly updates variables to approximate a target distribution, and the choice of update order affects sampling quality. This paper turns Dobrushin’s pairwise influence matrix, traditionally used to analyze convergence, into a practical tool for improving that order. The resulting methods are called Dobrushin-optimized Gibbs samplers, or DoGS.

DoGS tailors variable selection to both the available sampling budget and the subset of variables of interest. It also supplies explicit bounds on total variation distance to stationarity, quantifying how far the sampler may remain from its target distribution. The method offers certifiable improvements over standard systematic and uniformly random scan procedures.

The experiments cover image segmentation, maximum-likelihood estimation using MCMC, and inference in Ising models. Across those experiments, DoGS consistently produces higher-quality inferences with significantly smaller sampling budgets than standard Gibbs samplers. The contribution connects a theoretical measure of variable influence to concrete scheduling decisions, using convergence analysis to guide how a limited number of updates should be spent.
icml-2017-improving-gibbs-sampler-scan-q.tldr: DoGS uses variable-influence bounds to customize Gibbs sampling orders and improve inference under a fixed sampling budget.

paragraphs: When a person teaches an agent with positive and negative feedback, the meaning of that feedback may depend on how the agent currently behaves. Previous work often assumed that feedback depended on the intended behavior but was independent of the learner’s current policy. This paper tests that assumption directly.

The empirical results show that the learner’s policy influences whether trainers respond positively or negatively to a decision. Consequently, a feedback signal cannot always be interpreted independently of the learner’s current behavior. The paper uses this observation as the basis for Convergent Actor-Critic by Humans, or COACH, an algorithm designed for policy-dependent human feedback.

COACH converges to a local optimum, which is a more specific claim than finding the best possible behavior globally. The authors also demonstrate that it can learn multiple behaviors on a physical robot. Together, the evidence about human responses and the robot demonstrations support a learning formulation that accounts for feedback changing with the learner’s policy.
icml-2017-interactive-learning-from-poli.tldr: COACH learns from human feedback whose meaning depends on the learner’s current policy and converges to a local optimum.

paragraphs: Learning a ranking from pairwise comparisons requires deciding which pairs to ask about. The aim is to recover the order accurately while collecting few comparisons. When every comparison agrees with the underlying ranking, efficient sorting already solves this problem. This paper asks how useful sorting remains when comparison outcomes can be inconsistent.

The theoretical analysis gives favorable guarantees for Quicksort under the Bradley-Terry comparison model and natural assumptions on its parameters. These conditions are part of the result: the guarantees concern a specified model of noisy preferences. They provide a foundation for using a familiar sorting procedure in an active preference-learning setting.

The empirical strategy is particularly simple: repeatedly sort the items, using the sorting process to choose comparisons. In the reported experiments, it matches state-of-the-art methods, substantially exceeds random sampling, and uses a tiny fraction of the computational cost. The findings suggest that the machinery for selecting informative comparisons can be much simpler than more elaborate active-learning approaches in the evaluated settings.
icml-2017-just-sort-it-a-simple-and-effe.tldr: Repeated sorting provides a simple, computationally cheap strategy for learning rankings from adaptively chosen noisy comparisons.

paragraphs: Whitened neural networks transform their internal representations to improve convergence and generalization. The transformation also adds computational cost. An earlier workaround performs whitening only every thousand iterations, but the abstract reports that this allows poor conditioning to harm convergence. This paper develops generalized whitened neural networks to address that tension.

The proposed architecture learns compact representations, reducing the amount of computation required. It also allows whitening to occur at shorter intervals, preserving good conditioning instead of letting the transformation become too infrequent. These two changes connect representation size with the practical ability to keep the network’s internal representations well conditioned during training.

A further contribution estimates the covariance matrix independently of the data to improve computational efficiency. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate benefits of the generalized approach. The overall contribution is a way to make whitening more affordable while retaining the conditioning benefit that motivates it, addressing both the size of the representation and the cost of the transformation.
icml-2017-learning-deep-architectures-vi.tldr: Generalized whitened neural networks reduce whitening costs through compact representations and data-independent covariance estimation.

paragraphs: Training a deep network requires choices about the optimization algorithm, step-size schedule, and other hyperparameters. Exploring combinations can take substantial manual effort and computation. This paper develops a learning-to-learn approach in which a model learns how to optimize, building on the idea of using deep learning to exploit a training problem’s loss landscape.

The authors propose a new learned optimizer together with practical techniques for using it. The object being learned is the optimization behavior itself, making the training procedure part of what can improve through learning. This addresses the burden of relying entirely on manually selected optimization rules and settings for neural-network training.

The reported optimizer outperforms generic handcrafted algorithms and existing DeepMind learning-to-learn optimizers on many tasks. Demonstrations include deep multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and simple LSTMs. The wording matters: the advantage is reported across many evaluated tasks, rather than asserted for every optimization problem. These results support learned optimization across several neural-network families.
icml-2017-learning-gradient-descent-bett.tldr: A learned optimizer and practical training techniques outperform handcrafted and earlier learned optimizers on many evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Electricity records may provide consumption totals over intervals when the desired output is a much finer time series. This paper studies reconstruction from those temporal aggregates. It proposes a matrix recovery method based on nonnegative matrix factorization, adapting the method to observations that combine multiple times rather than directly reveal individual entries.

That observation model is central to the approach. Existing NMF algorithms typically take matrix entries as input, whereas this method works with aggregated measurements of individual consumption. The recovery procedure therefore addresses the form of data actually available in the stated electricity-consumption problem, instead of treating interval totals as fine-scale observations.

The authors also extend the method to incorporate individual autocorrelation, using relationships across time to improve estimation. This extension uses a convex relaxation of quadratically constrained quadratic programs. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real electricity datasets illustrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines aggregate-aware factorization with temporal information to reconstruct finer consumption patterns from coarser measurements.
icml-2017-nonnegative-matrix-factorizati.tldr: An aggregate-aware NMF method reconstructs fine-scale electricity consumption and incorporates autocorrelation to improve estimation.

paragraphs: Finding overlapping network communities means allowing a node to participate in more than one group. Two approaches are nonnegative matrix factorization and probabilistic mixed-membership models. Each has a theoretical difficulty: general factorization methods cannot promise a global optimum, while standard inference for mixed-membership stochastic blockmodels does not guarantee consistency.

This paper connects the approaches by studying symmetric nonnegative matrix factorization under the mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel. It establishes sufficient conditions for the factorization problem to have a unique solution. Those conditions identify a setting in which the optimization formulation has a well-defined answer; they do not establish uniqueness for every network or parameter choice.

The authors introduce GeoNMF, a computationally efficient algorithm that is provably optimal and consequently consistent over a broad parameter regime. Simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate its accuracy. The main contribution is a bridge between an optimization procedure and a statistical model, allowing stronger recovery guarantees within the identified regime while retaining an efficient computational approach.
icml-2017-on-mixed-memberships-and-symme.tldr: GeoNMF links symmetric matrix factorization to mixed-membership community models, with optimality and consistency guarantees over a broad parameter regime.

paragraphs: Predicting a complex dynamical system involves reasoning about how states and actions unfold over time. This paper learns distributions over temporal segments instead of modeling only individual discrete steps. Future state trajectories are conditioned on past states, past actions, and planned future actions, making a proposed action sequence part of the prediction input.

The approach combines convolutional autoregressive models with variational autoencoders. It also learns a latent prior over action trajectories, giving the framework a model of action sequences alongside its model of system dynamics. The authors report stable, accurate predictions over long horizons in complex stochastic systems, including uncertainty and effects from collisions, sensory noise, and action delays.

The learned dynamics and action prior support fully differentiable, end-to-end trajectory optimization and model-based policy optimization. These uses provide the basis for evaluating performance and sample efficiency. The contribution therefore connects trajectory-level prediction to control: the same learned models can represent uncertain future motion and participate in optimizing the actions that produce it.
icml-2017-prediction-and-control-with-te.tldr: Temporal segment models learn uncertain future trajectories and action priors for long-horizon prediction and differentiable control.

paragraphs: Reusing a feature representation learned on one task is a common way to approach another task. Neural-network weights and word embeddings are examples. This paper asks when such transfer can be justified theoretically, developing sufficient conditions that connect a source representation to bounds on prediction risk for the target task.

The first setting keeps the transferred representation fixed. Here, the authors identify conditions on the relationship between tasks and use a VC-dimension argument to bound target risk. The second setting uses the source representation to construct a prior that is then fine-tuned with target data. Under suitable conditions, a PAC-Bayes analysis bounds risk in this setting.

The paper illustrates its bounds using feedforward neural networks and derives a practical weight-transfer approach that it validates experimentally. The two analyses distinguish retaining source features from adapting them using new evidence. Their conditions are sufficient for the stated guarantees, providing theoretical support for transfer in those circumstances without claiming that transfer succeeds only when those conditions hold.
icml-2017-risk-bounds-for-transferring-r.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions and target-risk bounds for transferring representations, both fixed and fine-tuned.

paragraphs: Co-training uses two views of data to train classifiers that exchange labels for unlabeled examples. Those generated labels can be wrong, especially early in training. Standard co-training retains selected examples without removing incorrect labels, allowing early mistakes to persist. This paper introduces self-paced co-training, or SPaCo, to address that problem.

SPaCo changes the selection process to a draw-with-replacement mode, allowing training selections to be revisited. The authors also give the procedure an explicit optimization interpretation: its steps correspond exactly to alternating optimization of a self-paced curriculum-learning objective. This provides a robust-learning explanation for a process that previously lacked a clear optimization model.

The theoretical justification uses assumptions employed in traditional co-training research. Its scope therefore depends on those assumptions, rather than applying unconditionally to any pair of classifiers or data views. Experiments show superiority over the compared state-of-the-art co-training methods. The contribution combines reconsideration of training examples with a formal objective, addressing both persistent labeling errors and the interpretation of the learning process.
icml-2017-self-paced-co-training-efbf50a.tldr: SPaCo revisits co-training selections and connects the procedure to a self-paced optimization objective to address persistent labeling errors.

paragraphs: Kernel approximation replaces a kernel calculation with an inner product between explicit feature representations. This paper introduces Spherical Structured Feature maps for shift- and rotation-invariant kernels and bth-order arc-cosine kernels. The construction uses sets of points on a sphere, making the geometry of those points central to the approximation.

The authors prove that feature inner products are unbiased kernel estimates when the supplied point set is asymptotically uniformly distributed over the sphere. To construct such maps, they use the connection between uniform distribution and discrete Riesz s-energy. Their coordinate-descent procedure efficiently seeks a local optimum of that energy; the abstract does not equate a local optimum with a global one.

The construction has theoretical linear space complexity and loglinear time complexity. Empirically, the feature maps outperform the other methods used in the comparison. The contribution combines a geometric construction, a conditional unbiasedness result, and an efficient optimization procedure, linking the arrangement of spherical points to practical kernel approximation.
icml-2017-spherical-structured-feature-m.tldr: Spherical Structured Feature maps use sphere-based point sets to approximate kernels with efficient construction and conditional unbiasedness guarantees.

paragraphs: Stochastic-gradient MCMC can make Bayesian inference more scalable by working with smaller portions of a dataset. Its usual independent-data assumption is problematic for time series, where observations are linked across time. This paper develops an algorithm for learning hidden Markov model parameters while addressing those temporal dependencies.

Two obstacles motivate the design: the model contains discrete hidden states, and constructing minibatches requires breaking dependencies within the sequence. The authors use a marginal-likelihood representation of the hidden Markov model and exploit the process’s inherent memory decay. The approach therefore uses a property of temporal dependence to make smaller-scale computation possible.

The method is evaluated in synthetic experiments and on ion-channel recording data. The results demonstrate effectiveness, with runtimes significantly better than batch MCMC. This supports the practical value of adapting stochastic-gradient sampling to sequential models rather than relying on an independent-observation formulation. The contribution joins a representation that handles hidden states with a strategy informed by how dependence fades over time.
icml-2017-stochastic-gradient-mcmc-metho.tldr: An SG-MCMC algorithm exploits memory decay in hidden Markov models to accelerate Bayesian parameter learning from time-dependent data.

paragraphs: A point inside a convex polytope can be expressed as a weighted combination of its vertices. This paper asks how few vertices suffice when a small approximation error is allowed. It gives a deterministic, nearly linear-time algorithm for constructing such sparse convex combinations, turning an existence statement into a computational procedure.

For a polytope contained in an ℓp ball of radius D, with p at least two, the approximation uses O(D²p/ε²) vertices for error at most ε in ℓp norm. The approach generalizes beyond the Euclidean case and extends to more complicated geometry, including approximate Birkhoff–von Neumann decompositions. The authors also prove the sparsity bound tight using binomial anti-concentration.

Experiments find much sparser practical solutions than previously known sampling-based algorithms. That empirical advantage complements the worst-case bound rather than changing it. The paper also applies its techniques to support-vector-machine training and rounding fractional points in matroid and flow polytopes, showing how sparse approximation connects to other optimization tasks.
icml-2017-tight-bounds-for-approximate-c.tldr: A deterministic algorithm constructs sparse convex approximations with tight ℓp bounds and extensions to other optimization problems.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a difficult probability distribution using a more manageable family of distributions. The family’s flexibility affects what the approximation can capture. This paper introduces variational boosting, a black-box method that progressively enriches the approximating class instead of keeping its expressive capacity fixed throughout the procedure.

The method starts from an existing variational approximation and refines it through a sequence of optimization problems. It expands flexibility in two ways: adding covariance structure and introducing new components to form a mixture. These changes let later approximations represent relationships and distributional structure that a simpler starting approximation may not express.

Because refinement proceeds iteratively, the method offers a trade-off between computation time and approximation accuracy. Users can devote more computation to developing a richer approximation. Applications to synthetic and real statistical models produce posterior inferences that compare favorably with existing variational algorithms. The contribution is a systematic refinement process that makes approximation complexity something that can grow during inference.
icml-2017-variational-boosting-iterative.tldr: Variational boosting progressively adds covariance structure and mixture components to improve posterior approximations.
